node.label: Canadian working-class history
node.period_rationale: Period 2 (c. 1970–85) is the formation of the new labour history: Copp 1974, Labour/Le Travailleur 1976, Palmer 1979, Kealey 1980, the 1981 exchange. Logan 1948 is an earlier institutional root; gender, Quebec and welfare-state work continue in period 3.
node.date_label: Earlier institutional histories (Logan 1948) · Labour/Le Travailleur founded 1976 · Palmer 1979, Kealey 1980 · debate over culture 1981 · gender and family 1989–93 · coverage through 2000, selected later works

date_span.basis: Selected publication and institutional milestones. 1948 is an earlier institutional history, not the field’s origin; 1976 is the journal’s first volume (journal archive and Crossref; Freeman 2002 on the founding); 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary.

node.description: Canadian working-class history took shape in the 1970s as a new labour history of class, culture and community, set against an older institutional history of unions, labour politics and industrial relations (Logan 1948; Abella 1973; Bercuson 1974). The Canadian Committee on Labour History founded Labour/Le Travailleur in 1976. Palmer’s skilled workers in Hamilton (1979), Kealey’s Toronto workers (1980) and their history of the Knights of Labor (1982) were among its early monographs. In 1981 Kenneth McNaught framed the contrast as ‘E. P. Thompson vs Harold Logan’ and, by a later account, objected that social historians took a revolutionary goal as history’s purpose; Bercuson questioned working-class culture as an explanatory framework, and Kealey defended class analysis and culture. Social historians of poverty and the state widened the field: Copp’s Montreal working class (1974), Finkel on business and reform (1979), Struthers on unemployment (1983). Feminist historians remade it from within: Sangster on women on the left (1989), Parr’s gender of breadwinners (1990) and Bradbury’s working families (1993). Rouillard wrote the history of Quebec unionism in French (1989), and Heron’s Workers’ Revolt in Canada (1998) took the 1917–25 upheaval as a national subject. Palmer’s Descent into Discourse (1990) attacked the linguistic turn in social history. In 2000 Morton argued that the journal’s founding team had concealed a decade of stasis. Later work turned to deindustrialization (High 2003), the history of the left (McKay 2008) and Indigenous labour and the settler order.
node.scope_note: A national research field within labour history. The ‘old’ institutional history and the ‘new’ labour history are positions in a debate, not successive stages; Bercuson and McNaught are critics (their 1981 essays are now checked through Bercuson’s abstract and Finkel’s account of McNaught), and Morton’s 2000 critique comes from outside the new labour history. Marxist and Thompsonian resources are documented by McNaught’s title and Kealey’s defence of class analysis; no single theory is attributed to the field. Gender historians (Sangster, Parr, Bradbury) have their primary placement in Canadian women’s and gender history; they appear here for their working-class histories. Quebec labour history in French (Rouillard) is part of the field and of Quebec historiography. Poverty and welfare-state histories overlap with political history. Immigrant workers (Avery) are in the immigration entry; Indigenous labour is a strand, not a claim of adoption. Palmer’s Descent into Discourse (1990) is placed here as a critique of the linguistic turn, not as a critique of women’s history. McKay’s left history is a post-2000 contributor row; his primary placement is liberal_order_framework.

strands.title: Unions, labour politics and industrial relations
strands.focus: Logan’s history of unions (1948), Abella on the CIO, communism and nationalism (1973), and Bercuson on the Winnipeg General Strike (1974): the institutional history against which the new labour history defined itself.

strands.title: The new labour history: class, culture and community
strands.focus: Palmer’s skilled workers in Hamilton (1979), Kealey’s Toronto workers (1980), their Knights of Labor (1982) and Palmer’s synthesis (1983; 1992). Kealey also engages the US new labour history of Gutman and Montgomery (1990, title-level).

strands.title: Labour/Le Travail and the CCLH
strands.focus: The Canadian Committee on Labour History founded Labour/Le Travailleur in 1976: the journal’s archive and Crossref date volume 1 to 1976, with Palmer, Kealey and Rouillard (in French) among its contributors. Freeman names Kealey, Palmer and Sangster among the founding generation. The journal is also the site of the 1981 and 2000 exchanges.

strands.title: The 1981 debate over culture and class
strands.focus: McNaught frames the decade as ‘E. P. Thompson vs Harold Logan’ (CHR 1981) and, by Finkel’s account, objects that social historians took a revolutionary goal as the purpose of historical writing. In Labour/Le Travailleur 7, Bercuson questions working-class culture as an explanatory framework and the priority of history “from the bottom up”; Kealey strongly defends class analysis and culture. Kealey’s collected essays (1995) reprint his reply. McNaught’s essay is read only through Finkel.

strands.title: Poverty, unemployment and the welfare state
strands.focus: Copp’s Montreal working class (1974), Finkel on business and social reform (1979) and Struthers on unemployment and the welfare state (1983).

strands.title: Gender, family and class
strands.focus: Women on the left (Sangster 1989), the gender of breadwinners (Parr 1990) and working families (Bradbury 1993). Sangster (2000) describes feminist challenges to the initially ‘masculinist’ shape of working-class history and calls to integrate race and ethnicity.

strands.title: Quebec labour history
strands.focus: Rouillard’s history of Quebec unionism (1989) in French; Copp and Bradbury on Montreal’s working class. Shared with quebec_historiography.

strands.title: Steel, revolt and national scope
strands.focus: Heron’s steelworkers (1988) and The Workers’ Revolt in Canada, 1917–1925 (1998), a national frame for the post-war upheaval (title-level).

strands.title: Discourse, stasis and critique, 1990–2000
strands.focus: Palmer’s Descent into Discourse (1990) attacks the reification of language in social history, a critique of the linguistic turn (Finkel). Morton (2000) argues the L/LT team’s domination concealed stasis and decline; Sangster (2000) records the feminist critique and the unsettling effect of post-structuralism and the left’s decline.

strands.title: Indigenous labour and the settler order
strands.focus: Lutz (1992) treats Aboriginal people in British Columbia as a labouring class. Burrill (2019, extension) proposes a settler-order framework that puts settler workers’ ongoing theft of Indigenous land into Canadian working-class history. The relationship edge for Burrill is the settler packet’s screq_rel_07, to be retargeted to this entry (Q33); this draft’s duplicate wcreq_rel_05 was dropped.

strands.title: Deindustrialization
strands.focus: High’s cross-border history of plant closures, 1969–84 (2003), after the main period.

strands.title: Histories of the Canadian left (extension)
strands.focus: McKay’s Reasoning Otherwise (2008), first of a planned three-volume history of the left from 1890 to the Winnipeg General Strike; read by many PhDs who engage working-class history.

extension_coverage.note: Selected post-2000 works only: High (2003), McKay’s Reasoning Otherwise (2008, Q31), Burrill (2019, via the settler packet) and Finkel’s account of Palmer (2021, used as a witness to the 1981 debate). The 2000s deindustrialization and oral-history work and Labour/Le Travail’s later debates are not reviewed.

relation_to_periods: Main-period entry formed in period 2 and expanding in period 3. Post-2000 selections (High 2003; McKay 2008; Burrill 2019 via the settler packet) are extension records. Labour/Le Travailleur’s 1976 first volume is checked in the journal archive and Crossref.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Thompsonian class and culture in Canadian labour history
proposed_relationships.map_label: Thompson and the new labour history
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: McNaught’s 1981 title frames the decade’s Canadian labour writing as ‘E. P. Thompson vs Harold Logan’, and Kealey’s 1981 essay strongly defends class analysis and the study of working-class culture. A contribution of resources to the class_culture_community strand; no claim that Canadian historians adopted one Marxist theory. PhD context: E. P. Thompson is cited by 106 PhDs 2009–2026 (candidates.csv), The Making of the English Working Class by 56.

proposed_relationships.relationship: A national field within labour history
proposed_relationships.map_label: Canadian working-class history and labour history
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Labour/Le Travail, founded by the Canadian Committee on Labour History in 1976, is described by Freeman as one of the world’s leading labour history journals, and Kealey engages US labour history (Gutman and Montgomery, 1990). The atlas’s labourhistory entry has no Canadian participants; this comparison links them without making the Canadian field a branch of any one national tradition.

proposed_relationships.relationship: US new labour history and Canadian working-class history
proposed_relationships.map_label: Gutman, Montgomery and Canadian labour history
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Kealey’s 1990 ILWCH essay on the politics and direction of Gutman’s and Montgomery’s US labour history (both on the atlas’s New Left roster) is a dated engagement. Title-level only; an influence direction is not asserted. Optional.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Feminist challenge to a ‘masculinist’ working-class history
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Sangster (2000): feminist challenges to the initially ‘masculinist’ shape of working-class history, and later calls to integrate race and ethnicity, shifted the field’s narrative and paradigms, integrating gender more effectively though not completely into class formation. A critique that also remade the field (Parr 1990; Bradbury 1993).
